The model's notes on the prompt; shared prefixes ride free.

keyTerms.definition: 2 * layers * kv_heads * tokens * d_head * bytes; the memory price of context.
A function call the model makes to itself: append, replace, insert, search.

recall.answer: Intuition: the model cannot hold everything, so memory is a hierarchy: hot facts in context, warm facts in an index, cold facts in a store. Equation: KV bytes = 2 * layers * kv_heads * tokens * d_head * bytes. Code: a memory action is a function call the model makes to itself. Observation: reuse and compression trade memory for correctness, and the tradeoff is measurable.
recall.question: State the four-way link: intuition, equation, code, and observation.

sections.title: Four-way link used in this unit

keyTerms.definition: System instructions plus FIFO message queue plus writable working context.
Unbounded text store for everything evicted from main context.
Tokens used over tokens available; triggers explicit page movement.

recall.answer: Treat the context window like RAM and the rest like disk. Main context holds what the agent needs now; archival storage holds everything else; recall storage holds searchable summaries. In the toy, 8 items stay and 12 are evicted.
recall.question: What is the MemGPT memory hierarchy?

recall.answer: Break explicit eviction: a FIFO queue with no pinning evicts the system instructions at turn 9. The model then manages pages it cannot see coming.
recall.question: What breaks MemGPT memory management?

keyTerms.definition: Memory work is function calls, not magic: insert a fact, search it back.
Stores one fact: archival_memory_insert("user prefers morning meetings").
How many ranked hits a search returns.

recall.answer: Core hands rewrite the scratchpad (append, replace). Archival hands store and search the big pile (insert, search). Every hand is a typed function call, and the trace of calls is the audit log.
recall.question: What are the agent's hands for memory?

recall.answer: Break the log: unrecorded actions put a fact in the scratchpad with no provenance, so nobody can tell memory from hallucination. An agent inserting every turn without searching has write-only memory.
recall.question: What breaks memory actions?

keyTerms.definition: Recency times reuse count; predicts which facts earn desk space.
Never evicted; pinning 8 facts at capacity 8 freezes the desk.
What this turn needs: small, fast, expensive per token.

recall.answer: A token in context costs attention over every future token plus money, while a byte in the store costs almost nothing until retrieved. Put a fact in context only when its expected reuse beats the price.
recall.question: What is the economics of context versus persistence?

recall.answer: Break the hotness prediction: a cold fact suddenly needed every turn costs a search per turn until scores catch up. Pinning everything freezes the desk and hotness never matters.
recall.question: What breaks the paging rule?

keyTerms.definition: A compressed memory of one corpus, learned offline; 512 slots replace 20,480 tokens in the toy.
The training recipe: the model generates its own Q/A conversations about the corpus.
Into KV parameters; naive next-token training teaches recitation, not question answering.

recall.answer: Train one 512-slot cartridge for the manual instead of re-reading 20,480 tokens per query: a 40x memory cut. The model loads the cartridge (a small trained KV prefix) and answers from it.
recall.question: What is a cartridge and what does it save?

recall.answer: Break corpus stability: a weekly-updated manual leaves the cartridge answering from the old edition. A corpus queried twice never amortizes training; full context is cheaper.
recall.question: When do cartridges fail?

keyTerms.definition: The model's notes on the prompt so far; still valid when a new prompt shares the prefix.
The new prompt's first m tokens match a cached prompt's first m tokens.
Processing the prompt's tokens once; the first request pays, the rest ride free.

recall.answer: In a causal transformer, token i's keys and values depend only on tokens 1..i. Shared first-m tokens give identical first-m KV entries, so the second prompt starts prefill at token m+1. The toy saves 200,000 tokens across 100 requests.
recall.question: Why is KV reuse valid?

recall.answer: Break positional consistency: a block cached at positions 0..1999 reused at 500..2499 is wrong, because KV entries are position-dependent. Fully distinct prompts never hit; the cache is pure overhead.
recall.question: What breaks cache reuse?

keyTerms.definition: Splice cached chunks in a new order with surgical selective recompute.
r: share of tokens recomputed; 0.15 in the toy.
Tokens with the largest KV deviation after a shallow recompute pass; the surgical targets.

recall.answer: Each chunk's KV was computed without its new neighbors, so cross-attention is gone. Recompute the first layers fully, compare fresh versus cached values, and recompute the top-r deviating tokens. The toy spends 371 units versus 2,048.
recall.question: How does CacheBlend fix spliced chunks?

recall.answer: Break concentration: every token's KV shifts a lot, so the HKVD set is the whole input and the method is full recompute with extra steps. Chunks that never repeat have no cache to blend.
recall.question: What breaks CacheBlend?

keyTerms.definition: |S cap R| / |S|: of what came back, how much was useful; 0.60 in the toy.
|S cap R| / |R|: of what exists, how much came back; 0.375 in the toy.
A bad first query is not fatal; the trace shows the refinement.

recall.answer: Retrieval is the agent's eyes on its own past. Precision asks how much of what came back was useful; recall asks how much of what exists came back. Agents usually need precision over recall for the top few.
recall.question: What do precision and recall mean for agent retrieval?

recall.answer: Break the index: inserts never reach the search index, so the agent's own notes are unfindable and it re-derives them every time. A query with no relevant docs must return not found, not a guess.
recall.question: What breaks agent retrieval?

keyTerms.definition: Amnesia on purpose: keeps the gist, drops the details, permanently.
Every compression step records what it removed; names loss versus absence.
|D cap N|: dropped facts that were needed later; 2 in the toy.

recall.answer: A summary keeps the gist and drops the details; the dropped details are gone and no prompt recovers them from the summary. In the toy, 10 facts become 3 lines, 7 drop, and 2 dropped facts are later needed.
recall.question: What is compression loss?

recall.answer: Break the log: summaries with no drop record make a missing fact ambiguous between loss and absence, blinding summarizer tuning. A summary keeping everything is copying, not compression.
recall.question: What breaks compression handling?

keyTerms.definition: No fact older than t is served; a 7-day TTL caps the damage in the toy.
Per-week rate s at which cached facts go wrong; 10 of 100 per week in the toy.
The fact carries the version of the world it came from; stronger than TTL.

recall.answer: Memory rots. Invalidation is the expiry date: a time-to-live after which the agent must re-fetch. Expected stale answers equal queries times the stale share; shorter TTL means fewer stale answers and more re-fetches.
recall.question: How does invalidation bound staleness?

recall.answer: Break re-fetch: with the source down, the TTL expires the only copy and the agent has nothing. A never-changing fact (a birth date) should be pinned, not TTL'd; any TTL is pure re-fetch cost.
recall.question: What breaks invalidation?

keyTerms.definition: Every cached entry carries its owner; a lookup matches the owner first.
Authenticated id t on every entry; lookup key is (t, content hash).
Must be verified; a public entry with one tenant's name leaks it to everyone.

recall.answer: The cache key includes the tenant, so a hit requires the same owner. KV caches are invertible enough to leak prompt text, so cross-tenant reuse without scrubbing is a data breach, not an optimization.
recall.question: How does namespacing protect tenants?

recall.answer: Break the scrub: a public system prompt containing one tenant's name in an example leaks it to every tenant. Single-tenant deployments pay namespace overhead, but keep it for the second tenant's arrival.
recall.question: What breaks tenant privacy?

keyTerms.definition: o: facts useful in both tasks; 8 of 12 in the toy.
i: transferred facts wrong for B; 3 stale facts cause 1 wrong step in the toy.
Task B starts with A's notes; helps when tasks share the world, hurts on stale facts.

recall.answer: Net gain equals overlap saved fetches minus interference times the cost of a wrong step. In the toy: +8 fetches saved, 1 step lost. Facts are labeled by source task and staleness is checked.
recall.question: When does cross-task transfer pay off?

recall.answer: Break the labels: the store drops the source task, so B-queries get A's facts at full confidence and interference is silent. Two identical tasks make transfer pure gain and verification pure cost.
recall.question: What breaks cross-task transfer?

keyTerms.definition: Run the same tasks, same agent, same seeds, with the memory on and off.
Memory off; the arm the treatment is compared against.
d = p_on - p_off; 0.14 in the toy with standard error about 0.09.

recall.answer: The difference between memory-on and memory-off arms is the memory's contribution. Everything else is a confound: better prompts, easier tasks, luckier seeds. The comparison is the only honest test.
recall.question: How do you measure whether memory helps?

recall.answer: Break matching: the memory-on arm gets easier tasks and the delta is fiction. An ablation with memory off but doubled context changes two things at once; the delta means nothing.
recall.question: What breaks a controlled comparison?
